children: “Dear Prime Minister Ambani, Please accept my humble apologies for not realising that you are the real boss of India.” — SpaceX and Starlink owner Elon Musk
“We welcome competition... Every player must serve the people of India and abide by the laws...” — Reliance Industries Ltd
“I think I am significantly ahead in the queue from [Musk].” —  when they individually fulfil the security conditions, they can start operations.” — Communications Minister Jyotirao Scindia

Welcome to India’s satcom wars. While bitter and sardonic, Musk’s X post jump-started a heated debate in India’s long-delayed satellite communication space. For five years, major satcom players have been waiting for the final regulatory go-ahead to launch commercial services. As the sole foreign player among the three entities closest to clearance, Musk was the first to lose his patience — lashing out with allegations that the Indian government was favouring domestic “oligarchs”.
However, his rivals and policymakers reject that narrative. They attribute the deadlock to a complex and sensitive issue: national sovereignty.

Indeed, back in February 2025, when Musk discussed Starlink’s pending entry during his meeting with Prime Minister Narendra Modi in Washington and followed up with a phone call in April, a high-level alignment on tech and space was on display. Policy tussles between terrestrial and satcom players repeatedly favoured the global players until last year.

In 2024, while terrestrial players called for spectrum auctioning, the government favoured the global practice of administrative allocation. In the next battle — over pricing — terrestrial players pushed for high entry barriers, upfront reservation pricing, or similar minimum costs to “level the field” for players who had incurred a heavy financial burden after 5G.
The pricing structure now awaits Cabinet approval at 4-5 per cent of gross adjusted revenue, easing the financial duress of new players.
In a last-ditch effort, telcos asked the government to levy an urban fee of ₹500 per user for satcom players. This was rejected and it appeared to be smooth sailing for Starlink thus far.

The momentum shifted this year, after geopolitical developments clouded Starlink’s chances of getting licensing approvals in India. The India-US relation, too, has been rocked by differences over visas, tariffs, and other issues.

As India doubled down on security checks, around June there were rumours of a regulatory freeze for Starlink, and by August the Indian National Space Promotion and Authorisation Centre (IN-SPACe) rejected Starlink’s clearance request due to security concerns. No surprise then that Musk cried bloody murder.
Security vs connectivity

Addressing Musk’s allegations of a bias, retired Lt Gen. AK Bhatt, Director General of Indian Space Association (IspA), says, “Whether those allocated licence are Reliance Jio or Eutelsat or even Starlink, security definitely becomes important. While technology is moving fast and D2D (direct-to-device) is on the horizon, a deliberation of security consideration does become ethical for any sovereign nation.”
Tony Azzarelli, Vice President of Regulatory Affairs and Policy for OneWeb (which is Mittal’s partner), also expressed “shock” at Musk’s claim of an oligarchy blocking Starlink’s licence.

“I would argue that we have been slowed down by the newcomers. Why? Everyone knows, just take a look at the geopolitical situation in India-subcontinent and in the middle-east, this has created anguish and fear to the regulatory agencies,” he said in a LinkedIn post.

While tactical, Azzarelli’s comment about new players and security concerns is not without reason. Shortly after the X outburst, Musk reportedly ordered the slowdown of a military-grade version of Starlink relied on by Ukraine, wreaking havoc in that country’s ongoing war with Russia, according to media reports. In the days that followed, the company and the US government took turns shifting the blame on each other. The incident and other similar ones in the past only served to underscore the dangers of handing over communication services to a foreign player.

Kutniti Foundation, a think tank focused on national security, went so far as to call Starlink a wolf in sheep’s clothing that adhered to its biggest customer and promoter, the American government intelligence and military, while disregarding the sovereignty and democracy of other nations. It cited the examples of Gaza and Iran, where Starlink has flip-flopped on its decision to provide connectivity based on its understanding with the parties in power.
An industry source told businessline that the Indian government had spoken with the company on certain access and compliance measures. Failing to arrive at a consensus, all players remain in queue.
Need for satcom

Interestingly, some players are not as perturbed as Starlink over India’s delay. During a session at the India Mobile Congress, Tarun Chitkara, Vice President–Regulatory Affairs, Airtel, acknowledged that D2D could be a game-changer, but only for the 1 per cent of the population that cannot access terrestrial services due to geographical or commercial reasons, making it a complementary service for existing domestic players. This appears especially true when considering that Starlink’s annual plan cost ₹2,15,600 for 50-200 Mbps last year, almost 10-14 times that of major Indian broadband providers, which can prove a major drawback in the price-conscious Indian market.

On the flip side, India may want to consider satellite communication as more than just another broadband market, says Akhilesh Tuteja, Partner and National Leader–Clients and Markets, and Technology, Media and Telecommunications, KPMG in India. Satcom can serve as strategic digital infrastructure, connecting the hard-to-reach segment, strengthening resilience and creating an opportunity for India to build capabilities for the world, if executed correctly, he argues.
“The challenge is not to choose between security and speed, but achieve both,” says Tuteja.

The Cabinet is expected to soon approve the Digital Communications Commission’s (DCC) suggestion for a spectrum usage charge (SUC) of 5 per cent of adjusted gross revenue (AGR) for satcom service providers, with a reduction of one percentage point for services in government-notified hard-to-connect and remote border areas. Until then, the satcom players are left playing the policy version of musical chairs.

title: Satcom war. Asserting sovereignty in low Earth orbit
